section-2: The two images of India studied in this course reflect two traditions in Indian sociology. The ideological image draws on the work of thinkers, nationalist leaders and historians who tried to describe the 'idea of India'. The ethnographic image draws on anthropologists and sociologists who studied actual communities through fieldwork, such as M.N. Srinivas, S.C. Dube, McKim Marriott, F.G. Bailey and Verrier Elwin.

A student who completes this course should be able to explain the main ideas used to understand India, to describe the basic social institutions of Indian society, and to show how tradition and modernity, unity and diversity, and local and wider cultures interact.
section-5: Every society can be described in many ways. A historian, an economist, a novelist and an anthropologist may each describe India differently. Each description is an 'image' that brings certain features into focus.

Images of society are important because they influence how people think and act. For example, whether India is imagined as a single uniform culture or as a plural society affects attitudes towards minorities, languages and regions.
section-6: Ideological images of India have been shaped by thinkers and leaders such as Rabindranath Tagore, Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru and B.R. Ambedkar, as well as by historians and social scientists.

Nehru, in 'The Discovery of India' (1946), described India as an 'ancient palimpsest' on which layer upon layer of thought had been written without fully hiding what was written before. This is a good example of an ideological image of India as a civilization combining continuity and diversity.
section-7: The term 'ideology' was first used by the French thinker Destutt de Tracy in the late eighteenth century to mean the 'science of ideas'. Later, Karl Marx used it to describe ideas that justify the interests of a ruling class. Today it often means any system of political and social beliefs, such as liberalism, socialism or nationalism.

In the study of India, ideologies such as secular nationalism, cultural nationalism, Gandhian thought, socialism and Ambedkarite thought have offered different images of what India is and should become.
section-8: The term 'plural society' was used by J.S. Furnivall, a British colonial administrator and scholar, in his study of Burma and Netherlands India ('Colonial Policy and Practice', 1948). He described societies in which different groups lived side by side but met mainly in the marketplace.

Modern pluralism goes further. It recognizes and values diversity and seeks to give each group equal dignity within a shared democratic order. It is different from assimilation, which expects minorities to adopt the dominant culture.
section-9: Indian pluralism is seen in its 22 languages listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution and hundreds of mother tongues. It is also seen in the presence of Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis and tribal religions, in thousands of castes and tribes, and in regional cultures from Kashmir to Kerala and from Gujarat to Mizoram.

Historical examples of pluralism include Emperor Ashoka's edicts encouraging respect for all sects and Emperor Akbar's policy of 'sulh-i-kul' (peace with all). The Bhakti and Sufi movements also brought communities together.

The Constitution protects pluralism through freedom of religion (Articles 25-28), the cultural and educational rights of minorities (Articles 29-30), linguistic states and special provisions for tribal areas such as the Sixth Schedule and Article 371G for Mizoram.
section-10: Benedict Anderson, in 'Imagined Communities' (1983), described the nation as an 'imagined political community', because members of even the smallest nation will never know most of their fellow members, yet they feel a sense of communion with them. Print media, newspapers and common languages helped create this feeling.

Nationalism can take different forms, such as civic or territorial nationalism (based on shared citizenship and political values) and cultural or ethnic nationalism (based on shared culture, religion or ethnicity). Rabindranath Tagore, in 'Nationalism' (1917), warned against aggressive nationalism that could lead to conflict between nations.
section-11: Indian nationalism developed in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries through social reform movements, the spread of Western education, newspapers, the founding of the Indian National Congress in 1885, the Swadeshi movement (1905), and the mass movements led by Mahatma Gandhi, such as Non-Cooperation (1920-22), Civil Disobedience (1930-34) and Quit India (1942).

Indian nationalism was anti-colonial and aimed at self-rule (swaraj). The mainstream national movement tried to unite people across religion, caste, language and region. However, it also faced challenges from communal politics and the demand for Pakistan, which led to the Partition of 1947.

Historians such as Bipan Chandra emphasized the inclusive character of the national movement, while others such as Partha Chatterjee examined how Indian nationalism both borrowed from and challenged Western ideas.
section-12: The Indian Constitution tries to combine pluralism and nationalism by giving a single citizenship and a strong Union while recognizing linguistic states, minority rights and special provisions for regions such as the North-East.

In the North-East, including Mizoram, national identity coexists with strong ethnic and regional identities. The Mizo Peace Accord (1986) and statehood (1987) show how regional aspirations can be accommodated within the national framework.
section-13: The roots of Indian civilization go back to the Harappan or Indus Valley Civilization, whose mature phase is generally dated to about 2600-1900 BCE. It continued through the Vedic period, the age of the Buddha and Mahavira, the Mauryan and Gupta empires, the medieval kingdoms and the Mughal empire, and into colonial and modern India.

Important features include philosophical traditions (the Vedas, Upanishads, Buddhism and Jainism), achievements in mathematics and astronomy (the decimal place-value system and the concept of zero), art and architecture, classical languages such as Sanskrit and Tamil, and traditions of tolerance and synthesis.
section-14: Indian civilization has been shaped by many influences: Harappan, Vedic, Dravidian, tribal, Buddhist, Jain, Islamic, Christian, Sikh and European. Examples of synthesis include Indo-Islamic architecture (such as the Qutb Minar and the Taj Mahal), Hindustani music, the Urdu language and the composite culture of many regions.

The North-East has its own cultural traditions connected to South-East Asia and the Himalayas. Mizo culture, with its Tibeto-Burman language, clan organization and later Christian identity, is part of India's civilizational diversity.
section-15: Examples of continuity include the use of ancient languages and texts in rituals, the persistence of festivals, the importance of family and kinship, pilgrimage traditions and the continued influence of epics such as the Ramayana and Mahabharata.
Continuity does not mean that things stay exactly the same; it means that older elements remain recognizable and influential even as their form changes.
section-16: Major periods of change include the rise of Buddhism and Jainism, the spread of Islam, the Bhakti movement, colonial rule and the introduction of Western education, railways and the press, and independence with its democratic Constitution.

In modern times, industrialization, urbanization, globalization, the information revolution and social movements have brought rapid change. Changes in caste, the status of women and family structure are major examples.
section-17: Modernization is often associated with industrialization, urbanization, literacy, mass media, scientific outlook, secularization, democracy, bureaucracy and social mobility. Scholars such as Daniel Lerner and Alex Inkeles described the 'modern personality' as open to new experience, independent of traditional authority and oriented towards planning.

Early modernization theory, popular in the 1950s and 1960s, saw modernization as a single path that all societies would follow, often modelled on Western societies. Later scholars criticized this view.
section-18: After independence, modernization in India was pursued through the Five Year Plans, which emphasized industrialization, scientific institutions (such as the IITs and national laboratories), agricultural modernization through the Green Revolution, and the expansion of education.
Democratic institutions such as universal adult franchise (from 1950), elections, Panchayati Raj and an independent judiciary are also part of political modernization.
Since 1991, economic liberalization, information technology, mobile phones and the internet have accelerated modernization. Digital India (2015) is an example of a recent modernizing initiative.
section-19: M.N. Srinivas distinguished Westernization (changes due to contact with the West, especially British rule) from modernization (a broader process that need not be Western). Many scholars prefer 'modernization' because modern institutions such as science, democracy and industry can take local forms.

For example, Indians may use modern technology and live in cities while keeping their religious practices, family ties and festivals. The idea of 'multiple modernities', associated with S.N. Eisenstadt, holds that there are many ways of being modern.
section-20: Edward Shils, in 'Tradition' (1981), defined tradition as 'anything which is transmitted or handed down from the past to the present'. Traditions include beliefs, customs, institutions, art, language and technology.

Traditions are not fixed. Eric Hobsbawm and Terence Ranger, in 'The Invention of Tradition' (1983), showed that some traditions that appear ancient were actually created recently. This shows that traditions are always being reinterpreted.
section-21: Examples of continuity of tradition in modern India include arranged marriages coexisting with modern education, joint family ties maintained across nuclear households, religious festivals celebrated with modern media, and traditional crafts sold through online markets.
In Mizoram, traditional festivals such as Chapchar Kut, revived as a state festival, and values such as tlawmngaihna continue in a modern, Christian and urbanizing society.
section-22: Milton Singer's study of Madras city ('When a Great Tradition Modernizes', 1972) found that educated, modern professionals continued to practise traditional rituals by 'compartmentalizing' their lives, keeping modern work and traditional home life separate, and by adapting rituals to new conditions.

Lloyd and Susanne Rudolph, in 'The Modernity of Tradition' (1967), argued that tradition and modernity are not opposites; traditional institutions such as caste associations can serve modern purposes such as democratic politics.
section-23: Yogendra Singh's 'Modernization of Indian Tradition' (1973) is a classic work. Singh argued that the Indian tradition was based on four principles: hierarchy (in caste and social relations), holism (the individual subordinated to the group), continuity (belief in a continuing order, such as rebirth) and transcendence (values beyond the material world).

He distinguished orthogenetic change (arising from within the tradition, such as Sanskritization) from heterogenetic change (arising from contact with other cultures, such as Islamization and Westernization), and studied change at both cultural and structural levels.
Singh concluded that Indian modernization is selective and adaptive: tradition is not destroyed but modified, and modern institutions take on Indian forms.
section-24: M.N. Srinivas, in 'Social Change in Modern India' (1966), developed the concepts of Sanskritization and Westernization. Sanskritization is the process by which a lower caste or tribe adopts the customs, rituals and beliefs of a higher caste to claim higher status. Westernization refers to changes due to over 150 years of British rule in technology, institutions, ideology and values.

Srinivas also introduced the concept of the 'dominant caste' (a caste that is numerically strong, economically and politically powerful, and locally high in ritual status) and studied the village of Rampura in Karnataka, described in 'The Remembered Village' (1976).
His work showed that change in India occurs through concrete social processes in villages and castes, and not simply by the adoption of Western ideas.
section-26: An ideological image represents India through ideas. The key ideas in this course are pluralism, nationalism, civilization, modernization and continuity of tradition. Each idea highlights a different aspect of India: its diversity, its unity, its long history and its change.

These images have been shaped by nationalist leaders, historians and sociologists. Nehru saw India as a civilization with 'unity in diversity'; Gandhi emphasized village self-rule and moral values; Tagore warned against narrow nationalism; and Ambedkar emphasized social justice and equality for the oppressed.

Ideological images are not neutral; they can be used to include or exclude groups. For example, an image of India based on one religion or language may make others feel excluded, while a plural image respects all groups.

In conclusion, ideological images help us understand the different ways in which India has been imagined, but they must be checked against the realities of social life, which is the aim of the ethnographic image.
section-27: India is one of the most diverse countries in the world. Pluralism means not only that this diversity exists but that it is recognized, respected and protected.

Historical sources of Indian pluralism include migrations of different peoples, the coexistence of many religions, regional kingdoms with their own cultures, and traditions of tolerance such as Ashoka's edicts and Akbar's sulh-i-kul.

Constitutional supports for pluralism include freedom of religion, minority rights, linguistic states, the Sixth Schedule for tribal areas in the North-East, and special provisions under Article 371 for several states, including Article 371G for Mizoram.
Challenges to pluralism include communalism, linguistic conflicts, regionalism and discrimination. Pluralism is strengthened through education, dialogue, equal citizenship and respect for diversity.
In conclusion, pluralism is essential to understanding India because Indian society cannot be described in terms of a single culture.
section-28: Indian nationalism emerged in response to colonial rule. Factors that encouraged it include Western education, the press, the railways, economic exploitation by the British (described in Dadabhai Naoroji's 'drain theory'), social reform movements and the founding of the Indian National Congress (1885).

The national movement passed through phases: the moderate phase (1885-1905), the extremist or assertive phase, the Gandhian mass movements (1919-1947), and revolutionary movements. Gandhi's methods of satyagraha and non-violence mobilized millions across castes, regions and religions.

Indian nationalism was diverse. It included liberal, Gandhian, socialist and religious-cultural strands. Leaders debated whether India was a single nation, a nation of many nationalities, or a civilization.

After independence, nationalism took the form of nation-building through the Constitution, democracy, planning and the integration of princely states. In the North-East, the relationship between national identity and regional identity has been complex, but democratic accommodation, as in Mizoram, has strengthened integration.
section-29: Pluralism and nationalism may seem contradictory, but in India they are combined through a model often described as 'unity in diversity'. The nation is defined not by a single culture but by shared citizenship, the Constitution and common democratic values.

The Constitution provides one citizenship, a strong Union and national symbols, while also recognizing linguistic states, minority rights, the federal structure and special provisions for tribal areas.

Tensions arise when nationalism is defined narrowly in terms of one religion, language or culture, or when regional identities become separatist. Peaceful solutions have been found through dialogue and constitutional accommodation, for example the creation of linguistic states and the accords in the North-East.

In conclusion, Indian nationalism is best understood as 'plural nationalism', where people can be both proud Indians and proud members of their community, language and region. A Mizo can be both Mizo and Indian.
section-30: Indian civilization is one of the oldest continuous civilizations in the world. Its history stretches from the Harappan civilization through the Vedic, classical, medieval and colonial periods to modern India.

Continuity is seen in the persistence of philosophical ideas, languages, epics, festivals, family values and pilgrimage routes. Diversity is seen in the coexistence of many religions, languages, art forms and regional cultures.

Indian civilization grew through synthesis: different cultures met, interacted and created new forms, such as Indo-Islamic architecture, Hindustani music, Sufi-Bhakti traditions and composite languages like Urdu.

Tribal cultures, including those of the North-East, are an important part of this civilization, though they have often been neglected in older histories. Colonial ethnographers such as J. Shakespear ('The Lushei Kuki Clans', 1912) and N.E. Parry ('The Lakhers', 1932) recorded aspects of Mizo society.
In conclusion, Indian civilization should be understood as a living, changing and plural tradition rather than a fixed or uniform culture.
section-31: Modernization in India began under colonial rule with Western education, railways, the telegraph, the press, modern law and bureaucracy. After independence, it was pursued deliberately through planning, industrialization, science and technology, land reforms and democracy.

Features of modernization in India include the growth of cities, industrial and service occupations, literacy, mass media, democratic participation, secular law and the rights of women and marginalized groups.

Modernization in India has been uneven. Some regions, classes and groups have benefited more than others, and traditional institutions such as caste, joint family and religion have persisted alongside modern ones.

In Mizoram, modernization came through mission education, Christianity, administration, roads, government employment and urbanization, leading to high literacy and rapid social change within a few generations.
section-32: A central argument of Indian sociology is that modernization does not simply replace tradition. Instead, tradition adapts, modernizes and sometimes becomes stronger in new forms.

Yogendra Singh argued that Indian tradition was based on hierarchy, holism, continuity and transcendence, and that modernization brought new principles such as equality, individualism and rationality. The result is selective adaptation: Indians adopt modern institutions while reinterpreting traditional values.

Milton Singer showed that educated professionals in Madras compartmentalized modern work and traditional rituals. Lloyd and Susanne Rudolph's 'The Modernity of Tradition' (1967) showed that caste associations could become instruments of democratic politics.
Examples include the use of modern media for religious programmes, online matrimonial sites that still consider caste and community, and the revival of traditional festivals in modern forms.
In conclusion, students should present modernization and tradition as interacting forces, not as complete opposites.
section-35: The word 'ethnography' comes from the Greek 'ethnos' (people) and 'graphein' (to write). Bronislaw Malinowski's fieldwork in the Trobriand Islands, described in 'Argonauts of the Western Pacific' (1922), established the method of long-term participant observation.

Ethnographers live among the people they study, learn their language, observe daily life, take part in activities and interview members. The aim is to understand social life 'from the native's point of view'.
section-36: Important ethnographies of India include Verrier Elwin's studies of the Baiga and Muria ('The Muria and their Ghotul', 1947), S.C. Dube's 'Indian Village' (1955), M.N. Srinivas's 'Religion and Society among the Coorgs of South India' (1952) and 'The Remembered Village' (1976), and F.G. Bailey's studies in Orissa.

In the North-East, colonial officials wrote early ethnographies, such as J. Shakespear's 'The Lushei Kuki Clans' (1912) and N.E. Parry's 'A Monograph on Lushai Customs and Ceremonies' (1928). Later Mizo and Indian scholars have written on Mizo society from their own perspectives.
section-37: The ideological image is 'top-down', based on ideas, texts and national ideals, while the ethnographic image is 'bottom-up', based on fieldwork and the actual practices of communities.
Louis Dumont and David Pocock argued that the study of India should combine textual (Indological) and field-based (ethnographic) approaches. This is also the approach of VAC 102.
section-38: The phrase 'unity in diversity' became popular in the national movement and was emphasized by Nehru. It describes how India's many groups share common bonds such as geography, history, culture, a common Constitution and economic interdependence.
Ethnographers find unity in shared practices such as pilgrimage, festivals celebrated across regions, the spread of epics, and the economic and social links between villages and towns.
section-39: Major forms of diversity are racial or ethnic, linguistic, religious, caste and tribal, regional and cultural. Census 2011 recorded 22 scheduled languages and over 19,500 'raw' mother tongues, which were grouped into about 1,369 rationalized mother tongues.
Each region of India has its own food, dress, music, dance and festivals. For example, Mizoram is known for the 'puan', the bamboo dance 'cheraw' and festivals such as Chapchar Kut.
section-40: At the time of independence, most Indians lived in villages, and Gandhi described India as living in its villages. Even today, according to Census 2011, about 68.8 per cent of Indians live in rural areas.

Classic village studies include McKim Marriott (ed.), 'Village India' (1955); M.N. Srinivas (ed.), 'India's Villages' (1955); S.C. Dube, 'Indian Village' (1955); and Srinivas's 'The Remembered Village' (1976).
section-41: A village has a territory, a population, families and lineages, castes or clans, an economy based mainly on agriculture, religious institutions, local leadership and a sense of belonging.

In Mizoram, villages traditionally had a chief (lal), elders, the zawlbuk (bachelors' dormitory) and community institutions. Today, villages are governed by elected Village Councils and have church congregations and YMA branches.
section-42: Village studies helped sociologists understand caste, family, religion, economy, power and change through direct observation. They also challenged older colonial views of the village as an unchanging 'little republic'.
Concepts such as Srinivas's 'dominant caste' and Marriott's 'universalization' and 'parochialization' emerged from village studies.
section-43: Louis Dumont and David Pocock argued that the village is not a self-contained unit and that caste and kinship connect villages to wider society. Many villages depend on towns for markets, jobs, education and health care.
Migration, mobile phones, roads and media have further reduced village isolation. Therefore, sociologists study villages as part of regional and national systems.
section-44: The word 'caste' comes from the Portuguese 'casta', meaning race or lineage. In India, the varna system divides society into four orders (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra), while jati refers to thousands of local endogamous groups.

G.S. Ghurye, in 'Caste and Race in India' (1932), described six features of caste: segmental division of society, hierarchy, restrictions on feeding and social intercourse, civil and religious disabilities and privileges, restrictions on choice of occupation, and endogamy.
section-45: Louis Dumont, in 'Homo Hierarchicus' (1966), argued that the opposition between the pure and the impure is the basis of caste hierarchy. The Brahmin, as the purest, is at the top, and the untouchable, considered most impure, is at the bottom.
Critics argue that Dumont gave too much importance to ideology and too little to power, land and economic relations. Others point out that hierarchy was always contested by lower castes.
section-46: Factors of change include constitutional abolition of untouchability (Article 17), reservation, education, urbanization, industrialization, democratic politics and social movements led by reformers such as Jyotirao Phule, Narayana Guru, Periyar and B.R. Ambedkar.
M.N. Srinivas observed that while ritual aspects of caste have weakened, caste has become important in politics. Caste associations and caste-based parties are examples of this change.
section-47: Anthropologists defined tribes by features such as a common territory, a common name, a common dialect, kinship-based organization, a relatively simple economy, their own religious beliefs and political institutions, and a sense of identity.

Scholars such as Andre Beteille and Virginius Xaxa have pointed out that many tribes are now highly educated and modern, and that the term should be used carefully. In India, the official category is 'Scheduled Tribe' under Article 342.
section-48: Census 2011 recorded about 10.4 crore Scheduled Tribe people (8.6 per cent of the population). Major tribal regions include central India (Gond, Bhil, Santhal, Munda, Oraon), the North-East (Mizo, Naga, Khasi, Garo, Bodo and many others), the South (Toda, Irula) and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
In Mizoram, about 94 per cent of the population is Scheduled Tribe, and the state has its own institutions under the Sixth Schedule, including the Lai, Mara and Chakma Autonomous District Councils.
section-49: F.G. Bailey's 'Tribe, Caste and Nation' (1960) studied the Konds and Oriyas of the Orissa highlands. He described a 'tribe-caste continuum': tribes and castes are not completely separate categories but are positioned along a line, with tribes having more direct access to land and segmentary political organization, and castes being more dependent and hierarchical.

Bailey showed how tribal communities changed as they came into contact with caste society, markets and the modern state, and how political identities at the level of the nation affected local life. Some tribes became 'Hinduized' through processes similar to Sanskritization, while others resisted.
section-50: Census 2011 recorded the following religious composition in India: Hindus about 79.8 per cent, Muslims 14.2 per cent, Christians 2.3 per cent, Sikhs 1.7 per cent, Buddhists 0.7 per cent and Jains 0.4 per cent, along with others, including tribal religions.
In Mizoram, Christians form about 87 per cent of the population according to Census 2011, with Buddhists (mostly Chakma) forming the second-largest group.
section-51: Emile Durkheim argued that religion creates social solidarity through shared beliefs and rituals. Max Weber showed how religious ideas could influence economic behaviour. Karl Marx saw religion as a reflection of social conditions and sometimes as a tool of control.
In India, religion shapes life-cycle rituals (birth, marriage, death), food habits, festivals, dress, art and music. It also influences politics and social movements.
section-52: India is the birthplace of Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism, and it has also been home to Islam, Christianity, Judaism and Zoroastrianism for many centuries. Tribal communities have their own religious traditions.
Religious diversity is protected by the Constitution through freedom of religion and the principle of secularism, which means equal respect for all religions.
section-53: Robert Redfield, an American anthropologist, introduced the concepts of Little Tradition and Great Tradition in 'Peasant Society and Culture' (1956). He wrote that 'in a civilization there is a great tradition of the reflective few, and there is a little tradition of the largely unreflective many'.

The Little Tradition is the culture of the village and folk: oral traditions, local deities, folk songs, folk dances, local festivals and customary practices. Examples include village deities, folk tales and local healing practices.
section-54: The Great Tradition is cultivated in schools, temples, monasteries and courts and is transmitted through written texts, priests, scholars and institutions. In the Indian context, examples include the Vedas, Upanishads, epics, Sanskrit literature, classical music and dance, and the major religious traditions.
Great Traditions spread across regions and give a sense of shared civilization to people who speak different languages and live in different places.
section-55: Robert Redfield and Milton Singer emphasized that Little and Great Traditions are not separate but continuously interact. This interaction creates a civilization that is both unified and locally varied.

McKim Marriott studied the village of Kishan Garhi in Uttar Pradesh and described two processes: universalization, the upward movement of elements from the Little Tradition into the Great Tradition, and parochialization, the downward movement of elements from the Great Tradition into the Little Tradition, where they are reinterpreted locally.
section-56: Channels of interaction include pilgrimages, fairs, religious teachers, storytellers, folk theatre, temple festivals and, today, cinema, television and the internet. For example, local versions of the Ramayana are performed in many regions with local variations.

In Mizoram, Christianity, a 'great tradition' introduced from outside, was reinterpreted through local forms such as Mizo hymn singing, the lengkhawm tradition (communal singing at gatherings, especially funerals) and revival movements beginning in the early twentieth century. This shows how a wider tradition takes local forms.
section-57: The ethnographic approach shows that Indian society is made up of thousands of local communities, each with its own customs, connected through caste, kinship, religion, markets and the state.
It also shows that change occurs differently in different places, which is why fieldwork is essential for understanding India.
section-59: The ethnographic image of India is built from detailed fieldwork in villages, castes, tribes and religious communities. It began with colonial administrators and anthropologists and was developed by Indian sociologists after independence.

Colonial ethnography included census reports, gazetteers and monographs, such as H.H. Risley's 'The Tribes and Castes of Bengal' (1891) and J. Shakespear's 'The Lushei Kuki Clans' (1912). These works provided information but were also shaped by colonial interests and classifications.

After independence, sociologists such as M.N. Srinivas, S.C. Dube, Andre Beteille and F.G. Bailey used fieldwork to study caste, village and tribe. Srinivas called this the 'field view' as opposed to the 'book view' of Indian society.
The ethnographic image is important because it corrects stereotypes, shows the diversity and complexity of real life, and reveals how national ideas are lived differently in local contexts.
section-60: India's diversity includes race, language, religion, caste, tribe, region and culture. Its unity is based on geography, shared history, cultural traditions, economic interdependence, the national movement and the Constitution.

Ethnographers observe unity in practices such as pilgrimages to sacred places across India, the spread of epics and festivals, inter-regional trade and marriage networks, and participation in national institutions such as elections and the armed forces.
Unity is also maintained by accommodating diversity through federalism, linguistic states, minority rights and special provisions for tribal areas.
In conclusion, unity in diversity is not just a slogan but a description of how India actually functions: many communities living within a common framework.
section-61: Village studies were central to Indian sociology from the 1950s. Important works include McKim Marriott's 'Village India' (1955), Srinivas's 'India's Villages' (1955), S.C. Dube's 'Indian Village' (1955) and Srinivas's 'The Remembered Village' (1976).

Village studies showed how caste, family, religion, economy and politics operate in daily life. They also showed that villages were not unchanging 'little republics', as Charles Metcalfe had described them in 1830, but were connected to wider society and were changing.
Concepts such as Srinivas's dominant caste, Marriott's universalization and parochialization, and the jajmani system (described by William Wiser in 1936) came from village studies.
Today, villages are being transformed by Panchayati Raj, roads, electricity, mobile phones, migration and government schemes, but village studies remain useful for understanding rural life.
section-62: Caste has been studied from different perspectives. J.H. Hutton's 'Caste in India' (1946), written by a colonial census commissioner, described its features and possible origins. Louis Dumont's 'Homo Hierarchicus' (1966) explained it through the opposition of purity and impurity.

Historians Bernard Cohn ('An Anthropologist among the Historians', 1987) and Nicholas Dirks ('Castes of Mind', 2001) argued that colonial rule, through censuses, ethnography and law, changed and rigidified caste. Dirks claimed that caste as we know it today was in important ways a product of colonial governance.

Sociologists such as M.N. Srinivas studied caste in villages and introduced concepts such as Sanskritization and dominant caste. B.R. Ambedkar criticized caste as a system of 'graded inequality' and called for its annihilation.

Caste has changed through law, democracy, education and economic development, but it continues to influence marriage, identity and politics. In tribal states such as Mizoram, caste is largely absent from social organization.
section-63: Tribes in India are very diverse, ranging from small hunter-gatherer groups such as the Jarawa of the Andaman Islands to large, educated and politically organized communities such as the Mizo and Khasi.

Approaches to tribal policy have included isolation (Verrier Elwin's early view), assimilation (G.S. Ghurye's view of tribes as 'backward Hindus') and integration, which is reflected in Nehru's 'Panchsheel' for tribal development and in the Fifth and Sixth Schedules.
F.G. Bailey's 'Tribe, Caste and Nation' (1960) described the tribe-caste continuum and showed how tribes changed under the influence of caste society and the nation-state.

In the North-East, tribes have often maintained distinct identities through Christianity, education and political movements. Mizoram's statehood (1987) and constitutional protections under Article 371G show how tribal identity is accommodated within the nation.
section-64: India is home to many religions, and religion shapes festivals, rituals, food, dress, art and social organization. Religion also provides moral values and community identity.

Ethnographic studies show that religion is practised in local forms. For example, Srinivas's study of the Coorgs showed the interaction of local and Sanskritic religion, and studies of popular Islam show the importance of Sufi shrines (dargahs) visited by people of different faiths.

Religion can promote both unity and conflict. Shared festivals and shrines can bring communities together, while communal politics can divide them. The Constitution's secular principles aim to protect religious freedom and equality.

In Mizoram, Christianity has become central to identity and community life, and churches influence education, welfare and social norms. Christmas and New Year are the major festivals, while traditional festivals continue in revived forms.
section-65: Robert Redfield introduced the concepts in 'Peasant Society and Culture' (1956), describing the Great Tradition as the culture of the 'reflective few', transmitted through texts and institutions, and the Little Tradition as the culture of the 'unreflective many', transmitted orally in villages.

Milton Singer applied these ideas to India in his study of Madras and argued that Indian civilization developed through the continuous interaction of the two. McKim Marriott, studying Kishan Garhi, described universalization (local elements rising into the Great Tradition) and parochialization (Great Tradition elements being localized).
Examples include local deities being identified with major gods, local festivals being linked with pan-Indian festivals, and regional versions of epics.

In Mizoram, Christianity was localized through Mizo hymns, communal singing traditions and revival movements, while traditional Mizo festivals and values continue. This shows that the concepts can be applied beyond Hindu society.
Critics note that the concepts may oversimplify and may treat the Great Tradition as superior, so they should be used carefully.
section-66: The ideological image offers a broad picture of India through concepts like pluralism, nationalism, civilization and modernization, drawn from thinkers, leaders and historians. The ethnographic image offers a detailed picture based on fieldwork in villages, castes, tribes and religious communities.
Each has limitations. The ideological image may be too abstract and may represent the views of elites. The ethnographic image may be too local and may miss broader patterns.

Together, they give a balanced understanding: India is a plural nation and a civilization that is modernizing while maintaining traditions, and it is made up of diverse local communities connected to wider structures.
Students should be able to compare the two images and show how concepts such as unity in diversity, modernization and tradition, and Little and Great Traditions link them.
section-67: Key thinkers to remember: Nehru ('The Discovery of India'), Benedict Anderson ('Imagined Communities'), Yogendra Singh ('Modernization of Indian Tradition'), M.N. Srinivas (Sanskritization, Westernization, dominant caste), Louis Dumont ('Homo Hierarchicus'), J.H. Hutton ('Caste in India'), Nicholas Dirks ('Castes of Mind'), F.G. Bailey ('Tribe, Caste and Nation'), Robert Redfield (Little and Great Traditions) and McKim Marriott (universalization and parochialization).
Mentioning these thinkers correctly, with one key idea each, will make examination answers stronger.
section-68: Useful structure for a long answer: an introduction with a definition; the main features or arguments with thinkers; Indian examples (including from Mizoram or the North-East); a critical evaluation; and a conclusion that shows the balance between the two sides.

Common examination questions include: 'Explain India as a plural society', 'Discuss the relationship between pluralism and nationalism', 'Modernization and continuity of tradition in India', 'Importance of village studies', 'Tribe-caste continuum' and 'Little and Great Traditions'.
